newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: FEATURE-Puerto Rico ponders past, present, future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Puerto Rico ponders past, present, future.

text.p: It has been nearly 100 years since U.S. troops landed on Puerto Rico and seized it from Spain, but politicians cannot agree whether to celebrate, condemn or just commemorate the occasion.
The question goes to the very heart of the Caribbean island's complicated relationship with the United States and how Puerto Ricans view their culture and their island.

U.S. Gen. Nelson Miles, a veteran Indian fighter, and his troops captured Spain's colony in July 1898 during the Spanish American War. After the war Spain ceded Puerto Rico to the United States along with Cuba and the Philippines, but unlike those two possessions it has not been granted independence.

Washington appointed governors for Puerto Rico until 1948 when island residents began electing their own. Since then a debate has raged over whether Puerto Rico should remain as a commonwealth, become a state or seek full independence.

Commonwealth advocates call the curent status "Lo Mejor de Dos Mundos" -- the best of both worlds. Puerto Rican residents were granted U.S. citizenship in 1917, they earn salaries in U.S. dollars but they pay no federal taxes. They can vote in presidential primaries but not in the general election.
Puerto Rico has its own Olympic team but gets billions of dollars annually in food stamps and other aid from Washington.
The island holds on to a Latin American culture with a U.S. economy. Its residents speak Spanish but watch CNN and other English-language U.S. channels on cable TV.
FEARS AND HOPES FOR ANNIVERSARY
Opposition politicians fear the New Progressive Party government of Gov. Pedro Rossello will use the 1898 anniversary to push for U.S. statehood for Puerto Rico.

"They are going to use public money and create a celebration, the spirit of which will be to try to influence statehood for the island," Sen. Eduardo Bhatia, a member of the pro-Commonwealth Popular Democratic Party, said.

A bill submitted in the U.S. House of Representatives by Representative Don Young, an Alaska Republican, would authorise a plebiscite in 1998 under which Puerto Ricans will choose among commonwealth status, statehood or full independence.
In Puerto Rico's last plebiscite in 1993, 48 per cent voted for commonwealth status and 46 per cent for statehood. Independence garned only a little over 4 per cent.
Bhatia sees the arrival of 1998 as an opportunity to showcase Puerto Rico's progress.

"I think it will not necessarily be a celebration but a commemoration," he said. "We will commemorate the beginning of the relationship that began in an incorrect manner but through the years was amended to correct the deficiencies and has become beneficial to both countries."

Bhatia questioned the motives behind a plan by the pro-statehood government to celebrate the anniversary. Sen. Kenneth McLintock Hernandez, whose New Progressive Party favours statehood, submitted a bill in February to spend $98,000 to create a commission to study the American landing and decide how to mark the occasion. The bill passed but was criticised by independence advocates for avoiding the term "invasion."
"This is very clearly the use of funds to try to get people to vote for statehood," Bhatia said.
SEARCH FOR NEUTRAL TERMS

I call it a disembarko (landing), a politically neutral term," McLintock said, comparing the 1898 landing to the allies' arrival in Paris at the end of the Second World War. "I don't think the Parisians would call that an invasion."

Statehood advocates said U.S. aid transformed Puerto Rico from a backwater known as "the poor house of the Caribbean" to a manufacturing powerhosue with a living standard that is the envy of Latin America. "Basic individual rights came about as result of the U.S. presence," McLintock said.

Independence activists, however, say there was no altruism behind the U.S. action. "The United States took advantage of the Spanish American War to seize a strategic power in the Caribbean," said pro-independence historian Ricardo Alegria.

Spain had already granted Puerto Rico home rule by the time the Americans arrived. While Cuba was granted independence after the war, Puerto Rico and the Philippines became colonies. The latter gained independence in 1947.
"I hope next year the United States becomes the great defender of liberty that it says it is and recognises that Puerto Rico should have sovereignty over its own land," Alegria said."
